summaries.summary: Speech-to-Text translation is important in scenarios like emergency calls and online courses, with cascaded methods dominant but end-to-end methods offering lower latency and theoretically avoiding error propagation.
Because large-scale ST datasets are hard to obtain, multi-task learning and pre-training use ASR and MT datasets, but common initialization creates a huge gap between pre-training and fine-tuning.
Subnet Waste occurs because the ST system reuses only the ASR encoder and MT decoder, discarding pre-trained subnets such as the MT encoder and its semantic information.
Role Mismatch arises because the speech encoder is a pure acoustic model in pre-training but must additionally extract semantic and linguistic features in fine-tuning.
Previous work trains attention modules separately for ASR, MT and ST, so the ST attention module does not benefit from pre-training.
TCEN reuses all pre-trained subnets, keeps subnet roles consistent, pre-trains attention, uses a CTC-trained ASR encoder, pre-trains text encoder and decoder on MT, then applies multi-task learning.
TCEN concatenates an ASR encoder and an MT encoder, omits an ASR decoder, works encoders in tandem, and reuses the pre-trained MT attention module in ST.
To ensure speech encoder outputs match word embeddings, TCEN shares the CTC projection matrix with word embeddings and lengthens MT source sentences with repetitions and blank tokens.
Experiments on the IWSLT18 speech translation benchmark show component effectiveness and improvements of 3.6 and 2.2 BLEU scores for subword-level and character-level decoding.
Contributions are explaining insufficient pre-training knowledge use, proposing a new ST model that alleviates existing shortcomings, and empirically evaluating it on a large-scale public dataset.

End-to-end speech translation maps acoustic feature sequence x to target translation y^t without generating intermediate transcription y^s, assuming ASR dataset A, MT dataset M, and ST dataset S are available.
Multi-task learning and pre-training leverage large-scale ASR and MT data through one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many strategies for ST.
A many-to-many multi-task model has two encoders, two decoders, and three task-specific attentions, and can be jointly trained on ASR, MT, and ST tasks.
Since A and M are usually much larger than S, models are pre-trained on ASR and MT then fine-tuned with multi-task learning, but suffer subnet waste, role mismatch, and non-pre-trained attention.
This section introduces TCEN's tandem two-encoder architecture and attention decoder, its pre-training and fine-tuning strategy, and solutions for semantic and length inconsistency.
TCEN includes speech encoder enc_s, text encoder enc_t, and decoder dec with attention att, disentangling acoustic and linguistic feature extraction while utilizing every pre-trained module.
Following BIBREF9 inaguma2018speech, TCEN uses a CNN-BiLSTM architecture where input features x of length T_x pass through two convolutional layers followed by max-pooling.
Max-pooling downsamples the sequence by a total factor of four, and the down-sampled sequence is fed into five bidirectional d-dimensional LSTM layers.
The speech encoder output is h^s=(h^s_1, ..., h^s_{T_x/4}), where each h_i^s is in R^d.
Text encoder enc_t has two bidirectional LSTM layers, consumes h^s in ST and e^s in MT, extracts high-level linguistic features, and faces semantic and length inconsistency.
The decoder has two unidirectional LSTM layers with additive attention att and predicts y^t by estimating P(y^t|x).
Here, z_k is the decoder RNN hidden state at step k and c_k is a time-dependent context vector computed by attention att.
Training splits into pre-training, where enc_s uses CTC on A and enc_t and dec train on M, and fine-tuning, which jointly trains ASR, MT, and ST.
To sufficiently utilize large datasets A and M, the model is pre-trained on CTC-based ASR and MT tasks.
For ASR, connectionist temporal classification (CTC) BIBREF8 loss trains the speech encoder, removing the decoder requirement and enabling enc_s to generate subword representations.
Given x, enc_s emits h^s, and a softmax classification layer predicts CTC path pi with labels from V_src plus the blank token `-'.
W_ctc in R^{d x (|V_src|+1)} is the classification layer weight matrix, and T is the total length of encoder RNN.
A legal CTC path pi varies source transcription y^s with blank tokens and repetitions, and the CTC objective maximizes the probability of y^s by summing legal paths.
Phi_T(y) is the set of all legal CTC paths for sequence y with length T, and the loss is computed using the forward-backward algorithm.
For MT, cross-entropy loss trains the model by converting y^s to e^s through W_E^s, feeding enc_t, and passing h^t to the decoder.
In fine-tune stage, the model is jointly updated on ASR, MT, and ST tasks, with ASR and MT following the pre-training process.
For ST, enc_s reads x and generates h^s, enc_t learns high-level linguistic knowledge into h^t, and dec predicts the target sentence.
Following BIBREF11 luong2015multi, each task has a training ratio alpha_i, and task switching selects task i with probability alpha_i / sum_j alpha_j.
Connecting two encoders keeps role consistency but causes semantic inconsistency between e^s and h^s and length inconsistency between their sequence lengths.
The countermeasures share weights between the CTC classification layer and source-end word embedding layer, and feed text encoder source sentences in CTC path format generated by a seq2seq model.
During multi-task training, enc_t receives e^s in MT and h^s in ST, which may belong to different latent spaces and force compromise that limits individual task performance.
To bridge the space gap, W_ctc is shared with W_E^s so W_ctc = W_E^s, and CTC path label probability normalizes the product of h_t^s and the i-th vector in W_E^s.
The loss function closes the distance between h^s_t and the golden embedding vector, encouraging h^s to have the same distribution as e^s.
Length inconsistency arises because h^s length is proportional to input frame x and much longer than e^s, addressed by training an RNN-based seq2seq model and replacing standard MT with denoising MT.
A CTC ASR model trained on A generates CTC-path pi_i by greedy decoding, and reversible operation S(pi)=(u,l) converts paths into unique tokens u and repetition times l.
Dataset P is built from decoded A paths, a seq2seq model maps y^s_i to u_i,l_i, noisy MT dataset M' is created, and about 30% pairs are sampled from M' after validation tuning.
Experiments are conducted on the IWSLT18 speech translation task, with competitive baselines reproduced based on ESPnet for fair comparison.
ST-TED contains 272 hours of English speech with 171k segments, with 2k dev segments and tst2010, tst2013, tst2014, tst2015 as test sets.
TED-LIUM2 is provided as speech recognition data, containing 207 hours of English speech and 93k transcript sentences.
ST-TED and WIT3 provide 130k and 200k in-domain MT sentence pairs, while WMT2018 provides 41M out-of-domain sentence pairs.
Speech preprocessing uses 25 ms windows, 10 ms steps, 83-dimensional features, normalization, 3000-frame filtering, lowercasing, punctuation removal, speed factors 0.9 and 1.1, and text filtering.
Subword experiments use English and German sentencepiece vocabularies of 5k tokens, while character experiments represent both languages at character level.
Evaluation uses LIUM SpkDiarization, MWER segmentation with RWTH toolkit, and lowercase BLEU as evaluation metric.
The method is compared with following baselines.
The vanilla ST baseline has only a speech encoder and a decoder and is trained from scratch on ST-TED.
Three pre-training baselines initialize the ST encoder, decoder, or both from ASR and MT models trained on specified corpora.
Three multi-task baselines use one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many settings with specified task weights and in-domain MT data.
Many-to-many+pre-training derives encoders and decoders from pre-trained ASR and MT models, while Triangle+pre-train initializes components from ASR and fine-tunes under its multi-task manner.
All baselines and TCEN use ESPnet, RNN size d=1024, dropout 0.3, Adadelta, initial learning rate 1.0, and a maximum of 10 epochs.
TCEN pre-training uses α_asr=0.2 and α_mt=0.8, while fine-tuning uses α_st=0.6, α_asr=0.2, and α_mt=0.2.
Testing selects the best dev-set speech translation accuracy model and uses beam size 10 with length normalization weight 0.2.
Table TABREF29 shows the method outperforms many-to-many+pretrain by 3.6 and 2.2 BLEU, with pre-training, multi-task learning, and char-level models discussed.
Table TABREF37 ablations show MT noise, weight sharing, and pre-training benefit translation quality, with pre-training indispensable for end-to-end ST.
Figure FIGREF39 shows TCEN achieves a better fine-tuning start-point and outperforms many-to-many+pretrain by about five points throughout fine-tuning.
The end-to-end model outperforms the simple cascaded model by over 2 BLEU and is comparable to cascaded+re-seg.
Early speech translation pipelines feed ASR output lattices into MT systems, with common ASR and MT models and noise simulation for robustness.
Recent end-to-end ST works use pre-training, multi-task learning, curriculum learning, attention-passing, knowledge distillation, ASR/ST data, MT data, and synthesized data.
The paper proposes an end-to-end ST method that reuses every sub-net and keeps sub-net roles consistent between pre-training and fine-tuning.
